title: Westbrook City Council — Regular Meeting

fields.Location: Westbrook High School (Room 114), 125 Stroudwater St. (Hybrid via Zoom)

note: This summary highlights the meeting's key discussions and decisions, with direct quotes and timestamps for verification — it is not a substitute for watching the full meeting. Summarization necessarily condenses and selects; for complete context, nuance, and anything not covered here, watch the full video at the link above. (Produced by: WestbrookCurrents.com)
attendance: Present: President Jennifer Munro, Vice President Michael Shaughnessy (arrived at 6:27 p.m.), Brian McCambridge, Victor Chau, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Gary Rairdon. Mayor David Morse also attended.

blocks.x: Mayor's FY2026-2027 Budget Address
Proposed FY27 Budget (Not Yet Adopted)
Discussion Summary
Municipal: proposed expenditures are $39,088,502 (+6.48%). Non-tax revenues are $21,888,623 (+3.56%). The net municipal tax need is $17,199,879 (+8.41% cumulative).

School (as of Apr. 3, not final): PreK–12 expenditures are $57,871,667 (+8.47%). Adult education is $662,508 (+6.52%). Non-taxpayer revenues are $23,129,659 (+7.69%). The net school tax need is $35,404,516 (+8.96%).

Tax Increment Financing (TIF) and county: projected TIF revenue is $7,235,128 (+6.62%). TIF means tax from new development that is set aside for that district's projects. The Cumberland County assessment is $2,413,846 (+12.37%). The Mayor attributed the county jump to lost federal U.S. Marshals Service revenue tied to the jail's housing contract for Immigration and Customs Enforcement detainees.

Bottom line: the total property tax need is $62,253,369, up $4,960,698 (8.66%). Citywide valuation, or assessed property value, is projected flat. Real estate gains are offset by declining personal property value.
This implies a tax rate increase of $1.30 per $1,000 assessed value (8.63%). That is about $463 more per year for a median-value Westbrook home ($355,160).

The Homestead Exemption is projected to decline from $22,500 to $20,750 (assessed ratio ~83%). A return to the full exemption is expected in 2029, after a 2028 citywide revaluation. All figures are estimates pending final valuation and the June 9 school budget referendum.

Staffing decisions: the Fire Department was allowed to make offers to all four qualified applicants, ahead of two additional retirements anticipated for 2026. Only one of the additional hires came to fruition. That leaves temporary authorized strength at 47 (up from 46). The FY27 budget funds making that 47-position strength permanent, since TIF funds can cover a temporary increase but not a sustainable long-term one.
Of two requested Public Services positions, a new Operations Supervisor was approved (funded nine months). An Equipment Operator I position was denied, to be revisited next year.
Project management of the regional fire training facility has been handed to Project Manager Robyn Saunders.
Key Decisions

Informational — no vote taken; budget referred (sent to a committee to study) to Finance Committee (see Referrals below). The referral passed by show of hands, none opposed. Mover and seconder unsettled: the minutes say Victor Chau moved and Michael Shaughnessy seconded, but the recording names Chau as seconder.
Action Items
None.
Proclamations
Armenian Genocide Commemoration Day & Westbrook-Gorham Rotary 100th Anniversary
Discussion Summary

Mayor Morse proclaimed April 24, 2026 as Armenian Genocide Commemoration Day. Councilor Turcotte, granddaughter of genocide survivors, read a statement on behalf of Dr. Gary Zartarian of the Armenian National Committee of Maine. The statement thanked the City for its continued annual recognition.

The Mayor also proclaimed recognition of the Westbrook-Gorham Rotary Club's 100th anniversary (chartered March 8, 1926). Past president and current secretary Christine Johnson gave a detailed history. It included the club's partnership with the Westbrook Regional Vocational Center since 1957 and local youth programs. She also announced the 73rd Patriots Day Road Race (Apr. 20) and the 32nd Rotary Classic Golf Tournament (Sept. 28).
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.
Action Items
None.
Fire Department Staffing: Chief's Statement & Firefighter Testimony

Fire Chief Stephen Sloan opened with a prepared statement. It added context to his own March 30 WMTW interview. That interview stemmed from a firefighters' union Facebook post about two recent structure fires.
The first was at 71 North Street on Mar. 19. Nine firefighters were on duty citywide, responding to several calls at once, with Engine 3 on scene within six minutes.
The second was at Chestnut Street on Mar. 28. Nine firefighters were on scene within six minutes. There was mutual aid (help from neighboring departments) at both.

Sloan disputed a claim that staffing hasn't increased since 2004. He noted growth from 4 full-time members per shift (24 total) in 2004 to 11–12 per shift (46 total) today. The contractual minimum of nine on duty has stayed constant.

Sloan called mutual aid a normal regional function in which towns help one another. He said any staffing increase must be strategic and financially sustainable. He cited comparable staffing in Biddeford, Brunswick, Saco, and Scarborough.

A succession of current and retired firefighters presented a more urgent picture during public comment. Several identified with Teamsters Local 340 and the Westbrook Professional Firefighters Association (WPFA).

“This media release is a response to the statement issued by the City of Westbrook on March 31st, which seems to be a political walk back in the softening tone of the interview from Chief Sloan on WMTW on March 30th. Though WPFA stands in behind and supports the comments during that initial interview... The figure [nine firefighters] is only accurate if there is no vacations, no medical leave... In reality, staffing levels frequently operate at the minimum of nine... for 68% of the time last year. In 2001, the department responded to 3,000 calls for service, and last year we exceeded 5,200 with the same level of minimum staffing.”
blocks.cite: Captain Joe Carroll, reading a WPFA/Teamsters Local 340 press release

blocks.x: “Minimum staffing is not a savings account, it is a liability... We did however lose that bet on March 19, 2026, as you all heard, on North Street, when all available resources were committed on other emergencies. The same happened five years previous on April 9, 2021, on Spears Street, when only Engine 3 with two members arrived at a house fire with reported and confirmed victim entrapment.”

“68% of the time, this department operates with only nine firefighters on duty in the entire city... This is not new. We have been understaffed at multiple critical incidents in my short tenure... This very building we're in right now, we showed up with a minimum when there was a fire two floors above us.”
blocks.cite: Firefighter Adam Vining (on duty during the North Street fire)

blocks.x: Carroll's release also said the rise to 46 full-time firefighters largely came from converting per diem positions (paid by the day) after that staffing program failed. It also said the minimum of nine has not changed since 2001.

Captain Mark Terriel, nearing retirement after roughly 30 years, described the first ten minutes of any call, before mutual aid can arrive, as the most critical. He said there are only two fire trucks and two ambulances citywide, and no incident command presence after hours.
Councilor Rairdon, a 12–13 year council veteran, said the growth gap between city-side and school-side budgets in recent years concerned him given the stakes raised.
In second public comment, Carroll clarified the evening's intent was to open a long-overdue collaborative conversation, not confrontation.

“It's important that these conversations don't start with a Facebook post... I'm open, and this is the memo that we received this afternoon, about an hour before the council meeting started, was the first request for collaboration this budget season... Joe, I would like to invite you, if you're free, you and I can have a sit down tomorrow.”
Key Decisions
No vote or formal Council action resulted from this discussion tonight.
Public Comment: Gorham's Proposed Amazon Warehouse
Traffic Impact Briefing from Gorham Residents
Discussion Summary

Josh Trombley and Charlie Hample, both Gorham residents, briefed the Council on a roughly 94-acre land sale. Gorham's Town Council approved it in August 2025 with minimal public notice. The land is for a proposed Amazon last-mile delivery warehouse (~150,000 sq. ft.) on Route 25/Main Street heading into Westbrook.
Estimates cited ranged from 1,100–3,000 additional daily vehicle trips. Speakers suggested most would route through Westbrook's Main Street toward the turnpike.
The project still requires approvals from the Planning Board, the Maine Department of Environmental Protection, MaineDOT, and the Army Corps of Engineers before the land sale is finalized.

Assistant City Administrator Jennie Franceschi confirmed Westbrook has been invited into the MaineDOT review process and will take part, with Director of Public Services Eric Dudley, to represent the City's interests on traffic impacts. No meeting date had been set yet. Councilor Turcotte asked about raising a previously-declined Gorham turnpike exit with MaineDOT. Mayor Morse called that “a can of worms” but said the City would flag any overlooked solutions.
Key Decisions
Informational — no vote taken.

Rebecca Spatella Promoted to Director of Planning & Code Enforcement

She succeeds Jennie Franceschi, who moved up to Assistant City Administrator (see the Mar. 16 meeting summary).

Order 2026-37 — Fowl & Poultry Ordinance (Tabled)

Updates the Code of Ordinances (the City's laws) to comply with a new state right-to-raise-chickens law. It prohibits roosters at residential properties, citing neighbor complaints relayed by incoming Animal Control Officer Brett Bissinet. It also caps residential flocks at six birds (twelve in rural districts).
Vice President Shaughnessy objected to the drafted 1,000-square-foot enclosure size for six chickens. Staff said the enclosure (coop plus pen) was meant to total at least that.
A councilor asked if it was a typo. President Munro wondered if 100 square feet was meant. Public commenter Steve Pulsoni read it as a punctuation problem describing a yard.

The Council discussed enforcement timelines, coop-height requirements, and whether to split off just the disputed provision. It then tabled the item, meaning it set the item aside to take up later. Staff are to review the requirement and return April 27.
Councilor Turcotte pressed for a firm compliance deadline once re-drafted, rather than case-by-case enforcement, citing fairness to complaining neighbors.
Key Decisions

Tabled, 6–1 (Councilor Chau opposed), to return April 27 after staff review. Mover and seconder unsettled: the minutes say Michael Shaughnessy moved and Gary Rairdon seconded; the recording has the reverse. For: Michael Shaughnessy, Brian McCambridge, Anna Turcotte, Amy Faulkingham, Gary Rairdon, Jennifer Munro. Against: Victor Chau.

Order 2026-41 — General Obligation Bonds — Canal Elementary HVAC
Found on page 73 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

Authorizes up to $428,445 in bonds (money the City borrows and repays over years) through the Maine Municipal Bond Bank's School Revolving Renovation Loan Fund. The money would install ductless multi-zone mini-split heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems at Canal Elementary School. Under this state program, the City is responsible for 51% of the loan. The state forgives the remaining 49% (and all interest).
Key Decisions
Passed first reading by show of hands, 7–0. Moved by Michael Shaughnessy, seconded by Victor Chau.
Action Items
None.
Order 2026-42 — Land Use Ordinance — Child Care Uses (First Reading)
Found on page 80 of the packet.
Discussion Summary

Amends the Land Use Ordinance to comply with new state law. The state law raises the number of children a non-licensed provider may care for. It also allows nearby public open space to count toward a daycare's required outdoor play area.
The amendment also permits child care facilities in all zones where residential uses are allowed. It requires a public hearing at the April 27 meeting.
Key Decisions
Passed first reading by show of hands, 7–0. Moved by Gary Rairdon, seconded by Michael Shaughnessy.
Action Items
None.
Referrals, Committee Reports & Adjournment
Budget Referral & Committee Report Cleanup
Discussion Summary
The proposed FY2026-2027 budget was referred to the Finance Committee for review.
Separately, City staff recommended removing several long-standing items from the Council's standing committee referral list. They were:
Residential Landlord Registration (pending state-level action).
Austin Street Extension.
Central Street Traffic Concerns.
Councilor McCambridge objected to also removing Haskell Street Traffic Calming, questioning the validity of an earlier traffic study conducted during nearby road construction.

Councilor Chau agreed, saying Haskell Street has drawn many resident complaints over the years and residents were repeatedly told a solution was coming. He asked to keep the item on the list so residents would know the Council was not giving up. The Council amended the motion to keep that item on the list.
Key Decisions

Residential Landlord Registration, Austin Street Extension, and Central Street Traffic Concerns removed from committee, by unanimous show of hands. Moved by Gary Rairdon; seconder unsettled (the minutes say Victor Chau, the recording Amy Faulkingham).
Haskell Street Traffic Calming retained on the committee list at the request of Councilors McCambridge and Chau.
Action Items
None.
